title: Composite foreign keys generate as separate single-column constraints and will not map
description:
`_render_columns` attaches a `ForeignKey` to each column of a foreign key independently, so a two-column reference emits two single-column constraints rather than one `ForeignKeyConstraint`:

```python
RegionId: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(
    BigInteger(),
    ForeignKey(f"{SCHEMA_DBO}.District.RegionId"),
    nullable=True,
)
DistrictId: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(
    BigInteger(),
    ForeignKey(f"{SCHEMA_DBO}.District.DistrictId"),
    nullable=True,
)
```

That is two claims — `RegionId` alone references `District`, and `DistrictId` alone references `District` — where the operator declared one claim about the pair.

The package does not map. `configure_mappers()` raises before any query runs:

```
sqlalchemy.exc.AmbiguousForeignKeysError: Could not determine join condition
between parent/child tables on relationship Ledger.district - there are
multiple foreign key paths linking the tables.
```

The DDL is wrong too, and wrong in a way SQL Server will reject: a single-column `FOREIGN KEY` cannot reference one column of a composite primary key.

Composite keys are the documented way to express a reference `infer` will not propose, and the guide tells operators to write them in the overlay. What it does not say is that the result will not import.

## The fix

Render a composite foreign key as one `ForeignKeyConstraint` in `__table_args__` rather than as per-column `ForeignKey` arguments. Single-column references should keep the inline form, which reads better and is what most tables use.

`__table_args__` already carries the schema, so it becomes a tuple with the constraints ahead of the dict. The relationship for a composite reference then resolves from the one constraint without needing `foreign_keys`.

## Done when

A spec with a two-column reference generates a package that imports, passes `stele check`, and emits a single `FOREIGN KEY (a, b) REFERENCES t (a, b)` in the replica DDL, with a test covering all three.
close_reason: A multi-column reference renders as one ForeignKeyConstraint in __table_args__; single-column references keep the inline form. Covered at all three layers: emitted code, configure_mappers, and a single FOREIGN KEY clause over the pair in the replica DDL.

title: CI does not record or name the Python version the suite runs on
description:
The checks list reads as though the suite runs on 3.11 only. It does not: `check` runs everything - format, lint, prose, zizmor, mypy, pytest and the docs build - and `tests (3.11)` re-runs pytest alone against the floor declared by `requires-python = ">=3.11"`. The floor job is worth keeping while that claim stands; the install documentation makes a deliberate case for 3.11, so it is a promise rather than an accident.

Three things are wrong with how that is expressed.

**The interpreter is never recorded.** `check.sh` runs `uv sync --quiet`, which suppresses the line naming the Python it resolved, so no CI run says which version ran the suite. Reading the logs of a green run does not establish it; it has to be inferred from `.python-version`.

**The version the suite runs on is a file nobody reads.** `.python-version` holds `3.14` and is committed, and `uv` honours it. Delete that file and CI silently starts testing whatever the runner image ships, with nothing in the workflow to say otherwise.

**Only the floor job carries a version in its name.** So the one number visible on a pull request is the one that matters least.

## The fix

- Print the interpreter version as a step in `check.sh`, so every run records what it ran on.
- Name the version in `ci.yml` rather than relying on `.python-version` alone, so deleting that file breaks the workflow instead of quietly changing what it tests.
- Rename the jobs to `check (3.14)` and `tests (3.11 floor)`.

## The separate question

Whether `requires-python = ">=3.11"` is still the floor worth defending. Raising it to 3.12 or 3.13 would remove a job and a claim. That is a product decision rather than a CI one, and it should be made on whether anyone is expected to install on 3.11 - not on the cost of the job, which is fifteen seconds.

## Done when

A CI run states which Python ran the suite, the workflow names the version rather than inheriting it, and the job names say which is which.

title: Decide whether Binding.scalars and Binding.rows should preserve the element type
description:
`Binding.scalars` takes an `Executable` and returns `list[Any]`; `Binding.rows` returns `Sequence[Row[Any]]`. A caller writing `binding.scalars(select(Customer))` gets `list[Any]` rather than `list[Customer]`, so nothing downstream of the query is checked.

The generic form that would carry the element type through is spelled differently across the supported range: `Select[tuple[T]]` on SQLAlchemy 2.0, `Select[T]` on 2.1. The dependency is `sqlalchemy>=2.0.21` with no upper bound, so a single spelling is wrong on one side of that range.

Options:

- Pin `sqlalchemy>=2.0.21,<2.1` and use the 2.0 spelling. Callers get real types; the project takes on an upper bound and the work of lifting it later.
- Leave the signatures as they are. No upper bound, no false precision, and callers annotate at their own call sites when they care.
- Look for a spelling that holds across both, or overloads selected by a `TYPE_CHECKING` version test. Worth a short spike before committing to either option above.

The design posture on a pre-1.0 project favours the cleanest end state over compatibility with our own past, but an upper bound on a dependency is a cost paid by every downstream install, not just by us.

Done when the decision is recorded here and either the pin plus generic signatures land, or this ticket is closed as deliberately unchanged.
close_reason: Binding.scalars takes Select[tuple[T]] and returns list[T]; Binding.rows takes Select[Ts] bound to tuple and returns Sequence[Row[Ts]]. No upper bound on sqlalchemy.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text:
Measured under both versions rather than assumed. On 2.0.52, select(Customer) is Select[tuple[Customer]] and select(a, b) is Select[tuple[int, str]]. On 2.1.0b3, Select is variadic: Select[Customer] and Select[int, str]. So no single spelling covers both — the 2.1 form is rejected on 2.0 at the definition ("Type argument T of Select must be a subtype of tuple[Any, ...]"), not just at the call site, which also rules out overloads. A TYPE_CHECKING constant driven by mypy --always-true would work but makes check.sh depend on which SQLAlchemy is installed.

Taking the 2.0 spelling with no upper bound. The pin buys nothing: 2.1 is still 2.1.0b3, neither uv nor pip resolves a pre-release unless asked, and binding.py has 'from __future__ import annotations' so these annotations never evaluate at run time. Installing 2.1 produces a mypy error in one file with a one-line fix, never a crash. The bound is a maintenance obligation with no matching risk.

Separately: the SCD2 helpers in runtime/history.py return Select[Any], so as_of/current/versions_of erase the element type before it reaches Binding. Typing Binding only helps hand-written select(Model) calls until that is fixed too.

title: SCD2 interval settings disagree with each other and are untested
description:
Two inconsistencies in `runtime/history.py`, neither covered by a behavioural test.

**A sentinel-mode row with a NULL end is current but valid at no instant.** `_is_open` accepts `end IS NULL` as open whatever the mode. `valid_at` adds the NULL branch only when `end_open == "null"`. So in a sentinel catalog a NULL-ended row comes back from `current()` and is excluded from `as_of()` at every instant, including now.

**`overlaps()` ignores `interval="closed"`.** It uses `end > a` unconditionally, while `valid_at` switches to `end >= at` for a closed interval. A row ending exactly at a window's start is valid at that instant but does not overlap a window beginning there.

Both are wrong answers rather than errors, in the code whose whole reason for existing is that these settings produce wrong answers rather than errors when guessed.

`test_closed_interval_changes_boundary` asserts only that `interval="closed"` appears in the generated text, so it would pass with the boundary logic inverted. Nothing exercises `end_open="sentinel"` at all.

## Direction

Decide one rule for NULL ends in sentinel mode and apply it in both places. Make `overlaps` read `cfg.interval` the way `valid_at` does. Then add tests that execute queries against data spanning a boundary, for each of the four configurations.

## Done when

The four configurations each have a test that runs a query and asserts which rows come back, and the two inconsistencies are gone.

title: to_dict and __repr__ read column names rather than attribute names
description:
`Base.to_dict` and `Base.__repr__` in `runtime/base.py` use `getattr(self, col.name, None)`. The default swallows the miss, so any renamed attribute reports `None` for a populated field.

Confirmed: an object with `ThingId=7` reprs as `<Thing Thing Id=None>` and `to_dict()` returns every value as `None`.

This bites every column whose attribute name differs from its column name: keyword-suffixed names, any name that is not a valid identifier, and all of `--snake-case`.

## Direction

Iterate `self.__mapper__.column_attrs` and read `attr.key`. Drop the `None` default so a genuine miss raises rather than being reported as data.

## Done when

Both methods report real values for a class whose attribute names differ from its column names, with a test covering it.

title: The generated classes' convenience methods are undocumented
description:
`Base` gives every generated class two convenience methods, and neither appears anywhere in the guide. `rg -i 'to_dict|__repr__'` across `docs/`, `README.md` and `examples/` returns nothing.

`to_dict()` returns the mapped column values keyed by the names the class answers to, which makes the result usable as constructor keyword arguments, and takes `include_none` to drop null-valued entries. `__repr__` names the primary key by its attribute name. Both read attributes rather than column names, which matters on any class where the two differ - a keyword-suffixed name, a column that is not a valid identifier, or anything generated with `--snake-case`.

That rule is worth stating once where someone reading the generated package will find it, rather than leaving it in a docstring nobody opens.

## Where

`docs/generated/index.md` covers bindings, sessions and the schema token, and is where someone arriving at the generated package reads about what the classes can do. A short section there, with an example showing a class whose attribute names differ from its column names, so the rule is visible rather than asserted.

Worth checking at the same time whether anything else on `Base` deserves a mention, and whether the round trip through `to_dict` is a pattern the guide should recommend or merely describe.

## Done when

The guide states what both methods return and which names they use, with an example where the two differ.

title: A relationship attribute silently removes a column of the same name
description:
Nothing checks a relationship's attribute name against the column attribute names on the same class. When they collide, the class body has two assignments under one name, the relationship wins, and declarative never sees the `mapped_column`.

Confirmed: a table with a column named `h4_owner` alongside a foreign key whose relationship is also named `h4_owner` generates a class whose mapped columns are `['H4OwnerId', 'H4PetId']`. The column is gone from the mapping and from the replica DDL, and `stele check` passes.

The fixed `history` attribute on a primary class has the same hazard against a column named `history`.

Column names come from a customer catalog, relationship names are derived from table names, and nothing prevents them meeting. The failure is silent, which is the class of failure this tool exists to avoid.

## Direction

Collect the column attribute names before rendering relationships, and on collision either suffix the relationship name or refuse, in both cases with a line in the generation report.

## Done when

A spec whose column name collides with a derived relationship name generates a class that keeps the column, and the collision is reported.
close_reason: A relationship whose name matches a column on either side is not generated, and the reason is reported. The column is the data; the overlay's relationship_name and backref_name are the way to keep both.

title: Primary key inference only recognises key names built as a suffix
description:
`_pk_candidates` recognises a key column three ways, and all three assume the key name is built by appending to the table name:

- `_key_suffixes(table_name)`, which is the table name and a naive singular of it, each concatenated with `id`, `key`, `code`, `no`, `num`, or `sk`.
- A bare generic name — `id`, `key`, `sk`, `rowid`, `guid`, `uuid` — in one of the first three ordinal positions.
- A name ending in `id` whose stem prefixes the table name.

A schema that names its keys the other way round, `IdObjectType` rather than `ObjectTypeId`, matches none of them. Confirmed by running the heuristics over a two-schema spec: a suffix-style `Widget`/`Order` pair proposes `WidgetId` at 0.99 and the foreign key at 0.80, including across schemas, while a prefix-style `Gadget`/`Shipment` pair in another schema proposes nothing and both tables are left with no primary key.

The consequence is a cascade rather than a single miss. `propose_foreign_keys` only indexes a table that already has a single-column primary key, so a table whose key was not recognised cannot be a foreign key target either. A prefix-style schema therefore comes back with no keys and no relationships at all, not merely with some of them missing.

Foreign key matching itself needs no change. The target index already includes the parent's own primary key column name, so a spec that has the primary keys produces the relationships: setting `b.Gadget.primary_key` to `IdGadget` yields `b.Shipment(IdGadget) -> b.Gadget` at 0.80. The whole defect is in primary key inference.

## No operator escape hatch

There is no way to supply the missing keys and get proposals back. `apply_overlay` is called from `cmd_generate` and nowhere else, so `stele infer` reads `model.yaml` alone and never sees `overlay.yaml`. Keys written into the overlay reach the generated package but cannot feed the inference that would find the relationships. `stele infer --apply` writes accepted proposals into the spec, which does not help when nothing was proposed. That leaves hand-editing `model.yaml`, which the pipeline treats as regenerable and overwrites on the next `stele introspect`.

So for a prefix-style schema the overlay has to carry every primary key and every foreign key written out by hand, with none of the proposal or evidence machinery. Whether `infer` should apply an overlay before proposing is a design question worth settling separately; it is the general form of this defect.

## Options

- Add a prefix rule mirroring the existing suffix rule: the same six affixes, tried as a prefix on the table name and its singular.
- Infer the convention per schema by counting which shape fits more tables, and apply only the winner within that schema. Avoids `IdCode` style false positives in a schema that does not use the convention, at the cost of a rule that no longer fits in one sentence.

## Done when

A prefix-style schema gets primary key proposals, `tests/test_pipeline.py` covers both naming shapes in one spec, and the overlay stub still lets a wrong guess be overridden.
close_reason: _key_names offers the six key affixes on either side of the table name, so prefix-style schemas get primary key proposals and, through them, foreign key proposals. The FK target index picks the change up unchanged.

title: The overlay drops unknown table keys silently and applies scalars in an unstable order
description:
Two defects in `overlay.py`, in the one file an operator hand-edits.

**Unknown table-level keys vanish.** `_apply_table` warns about unknown column keys and unknown foreign key keys, but iterates `_TABLE_SCALARS` and never looks at what is left over. `class_nmae:` or `primary_keys:` is discarded with no output at all. `docs/overlay.md` states the opposite: "Unknown keys are warned about rather than ignored silently." A typo in a hand-edited file is exactly what that warning is for.

**Application order depends on set iteration.** `_TABLE_SCALARS` is a set, so when an entry sets both `primary_key` and `primary_key_origin`, whether the explicit origin survives the automatic `"manual"` stamp varies with the process hash seed. Across seeds the result was `manual, catalog, manual, manual, catalog`.

## Direction

Diff the entry's keys against the accepted set plus `columns`, `foreign_keys` and `foreign_keys_mode`, and warn on the remainder. Iterate a tuple rather than a set, and stamp `"manual"` only when the overlay did not set the origin itself.

## Done when

An overlay with a misspelled table key produces a warning naming it, and applying the same overlay twice under different hash seeds gives the same spec.

title: Annotate remaining functions and enable mypy disallow_untyped_defs
description:
The mypy configuration runs with `check_untyped_defs`, `warn_return_any`, `strict_equality`, `no_implicit_optional`, `warn_redundant_casts`, and `warn_unused_ignores` on, but `disallow_untyped_defs` and `disallow_incomplete_defs` off. Bodies are checked; signatures are not required to be complete.

Turning both on reports 29 functions in `src/` needing annotations, concentrated in `cli.py` (subcommand handlers taking a bare `args`), `runtime/binding.py`, `runtime/history.py`, and `db.py`. Most are mechanical — `args: argparse.Namespace`, `-> None`. The SQLAlchemy-facing ones in `runtime/` need more care because the useful types are generic.

Done when both flags are on in `pyproject.toml` and `./check.sh` passes.
close_reason: Signatures completed; both mypy flags on and check.sh green

title: Self-referencing foreign keys generate relationships that will not configure
description:
A foreign key from a table to itself generates a `relationship` pair that SQLAlchemy refuses to configure:

```
sqlalchemy.exc.ArgumentError: Account.parent and back-reference
Account.children are both of the same direction
<RelationshipDirection.ONETOMANY: 1>. Did you mean to set remote_side on
the many-to-one side?
```

`_render_fk_relationships` emits the many-to-one side and `_render_backrefs` emits the collection side, and on a self-join SQLAlchemy cannot infer which end is which without `remote_side` on the many-to-one side. The package does not import, so `stele check` fails before any query runs.

Self-references are not proposed by `infer` - they are real often enough to want and wrong often enough to want confirmed - so the documented route is to declare them in the overlay. Doing that produces a package that will not map.

The history side is unaffected: a history class reaches its parent through an explicit `primaryjoin` carrying `foreign()`, which tells SQLAlchemy which end is dependent without further help.

## The fix

When a foreign key's referred table is the table it is declared on, pass `remote_side` naming the referenced columns on the many-to-one side. The collection side needs nothing extra once the scalar side is unambiguous.

## Done when

A spec with a self-referencing foreign key generates a package that imports and passes `stele check`, and a test covers a parent-child hierarchy on one table.
close_reason: A self-referencing foreign key renders remote_side on the many-to-one side, so the generated package imports and stele check passes. Covered by test_a_self_reference_configures.

title: safe_attr accepts column names that produce invalid Python
description:
`safe_attr` guards against two things incompletely.

The hand-rolled keyword list omits `except`, `lambda`, `global`, `del`, `try`, `raise`, `yield` and `async`, among others. `keyword.iskeyword` exists.

The identifier check tests only the first character, so a Databricks column named `my col` or `my-col` - both legal there - is emitted verbatim as an attribute name and the generated module is a syntax error.

Loud rather than silent, but it fails at import with no indication of which column caused it.

## Direction

Use `keyword.iskeyword`, and validate the whole name with `str.isidentifier` rather than the first character. Report the rename in the generation output so the mapping is discoverable.

## Done when

A column named for a keyword or containing a space generates a valid module, and the rename appears in the report.

title: Generating with --snake-case produces a package that cannot configure
description:
`generate --snake-case` renames attributes but four places keep using the raw column name where the attribute name is required: the `__scd2__` descriptor, the history link's `primaryjoin`, the history-to-parent joins, and `remote_side` for a self-reference.

Confirmed on a `Gizmo`/`Gizmo_history` pair:

```
history attributes:  ['end_date', 'gizmo_id', 'gizmo_name', 'start_date']
__scd2__.start_attr: StartDate

AttributeError: Class GizmoHistory does not have a mapped column named 'StartDate'
```

A spec with no history pair fails later instead, at the first point-in-time call.

The flag exists for CamelCase catalogs, which is the only kind where it changes anything, so it does not work for its own use case. `docs/pipeline/generate.md` documents it as working.

## Direction

Thread the attribute-naming function through the four sites, or drop the flag and the documentation for it. There is no test with `preserve_names=False`, which is why this was invisible.

## Done when

A CamelCase spec with a history pair generates, imports and configures under `--snake-case`, with point-in-time queries working, or the flag is gone.
close_reason: One attr_name() method decides what a column is called on the class, and the seven sites that need an attribute name use it: the SCD2 descriptor, both history joins, the order_by, and remote_side.

title: add_tables cannot produce a class that maps
description:
`add_tables` creates a `TableSpec` with no columns, and there is no overlay syntax for adding any - `_apply_table` only modifies columns that already exist, and reports `column dbo.Region.RegionId not found; ignored` for anything else. The generated class therefore has no mapped columns and the package fails to import with `could not assemble any primary key columns`.

`docs/overlay.md` presents `add_tables` as taking "the same shape as `tables`", and suggests it for a reference pointing outside the mirrored subset, which is a real need.

## Direction

Either accept column definitions under `add_tables` - name, type, nullability, enough to render a `mapped_column` - or remove the feature along with its documentation. Half of it is worse than neither.

## Done when

An `add_tables` entry either generates a class that imports and maps, or the feature and its documentation are gone.

title: A pinned session is documented read-only but does not enforce it
description:
`Binding.as_of`'s docstring and `docs/generated/history.md` both say plainly that the session is read-only. The enforcement is `autoflush = False` and no automatic commit, so an explicit `session.execute(update(...))` followed by `commit()` writes through.

Worse, the pin's listener returns early for anything that is not a select, so a bulk `UPDATE` inside a pinned session runs against every version rather than the one the session is pinned to.

Only Databricks engines carry a write guard; a replica binding has none.

Given the project's rule about precision over reassurance, the wording is the defect even if the code is left alone.

## Direction

Raise `PinnedSessionError` from the listener for non-select executions, which is one branch and matches what the documentation already claims. Failing that, reword both places to say what is actually true.

## Done when

Either a write inside a pinned session raises, or nothing in the code or the guide describes a pinned session as read-only.

title: Several foreign keys to one parent generate a package that cannot configure
description:
Two foreign keys from one table to the same parent - the `BuyerId`/`SellerId` or `CreatedBy`/`UpdatedBy` shape, which is close to universal - produce relationships SQLAlchemy cannot resolve:

```
AmbiguousForeignKeysError: Could not determine join condition between
parent/child tables on relationship H1Party.bought
```

Neither `_render_fk_relationships` nor `_render_backrefs` passes `foreign_keys=`, so with more than one path between the tables SQLAlchemy has nothing to disambiguate on. Confirmed with derived names and again with explicit `relationship_name` and `backref_name` from the overlay, so there is no way out short of hand-editing generated code.

The attribute disambiguation is also inconsistent between the two sides. The child side builds a name from the column stem, the parent side builds one from a different rule, and every `back_populates` points at the undisambiguated name, so the pairing is wrong before the foreign keys are even considered. `docs/generated/relationships.md` describes the disambiguation as producing `billing_customer` and `shipping_customer`, which is not what the code does.

It fails loudly at `stele check` rather than silently, but it blocks generation for a common shape.

## Direction

Emit `foreign_keys=` naming the constrained columns whenever more than one enabled foreign key targets the same parent. Give both sides one shared naming function so the two ends agree, and make `back_populates` use the final names.

## Done when

A table with two foreign keys to one parent generates a package that imports and configures, both relationships resolve to the right columns, and the documented naming matches the code.
close_reason: Both ends derive their names from _relationship_names(), a pure function of the reference and the two tables, so back_populates always pairs. Several references between the same two tables carry foreign_keys naming their columns.

title: Smaller gaps in key and relationship inference
description:
Three narrow limits, none urgent, all worth a decision.

**A rejected primary key has no fallback.** `propose_primary_keys` proposes only the highest-scoring candidate. If `--validate` rejects it for duplicates or nulls, the second candidate is never tried, and because foreign key targets need a key the table also loses every relationship pointing at it.

**Columns in the child's own key are never foreign key candidates.** So an identifying relationship - a one-to-one extension table sharing its parent's key - can never be proposed. This may well be deliberate, but `docs/heuristics.md` says "Every column of every table is matched against an index of key names", which is not what happens.

**An enabled history table whose primary is disabled disappears.** It is only reached through its primary in `build_modules`, so it is not rendered; and `unpaired_history` does not report it because the primary still exists in the spec. Suspected from reading rather than confirmed.

## Done when

Each is either fixed or documented as intended, and the heuristics page describes what the code does.

title: Narrow history relationships through an as-of session context
description:
A generated history class carries no relationships, so every traversal from a version row is hand-written. The obvious fix is worse than the gap: a plain relationship joins to the parent's *current* row, so a version from January 2025 reports the region name as it stands today.

Measured on a model where region 3 was renamed from `North` to `Northern` in September 2025:

```
version interval           name       rid  naive relationship  point-in-time
2025-01-01 -> 2025-06-01   Acme Ltd     3  Northern            North
2025-06-01 -> 2026-02-01   Acme Ltd     7  Southern            South
2026-02-01 -> open         Acme Corp    7  Southern            Southern
```

The last row is why this is a trap and not a bug. For the current version both agree, so the naive relationship is right for every row someone checks by hand and for any test written against current data. It fails only on historical questions, which is the only time anyone asks it.

## The design

Generate the relationship joined on the **key columns alone**, with no interval logic, and narrow it with a session-level as-of context built on `with_loader_criteria`.

```python
with binding.as_of("2025-03-01") as s:
    for c in s.scalars(select(CustomerHistory)):
        c.region                      # the region as it stood in March 2025

binding.as_of()                       # now
binding.as_of(at, overrides={RegionHistory: other})   # a different moment
binding.as_of(at, overrides={RegionHistory: None})    # unfiltered
```

The context registers a `do_orm_execute` listener that adds one `with_loader_criteria(cls, cls.valid_at(at), include_aliases=True)` per history class. Measured to reach the top-level select, lazy loads, `selectinload`, `joinedload`, and joins written by hand: an explicit `select(CustomerHistory, RegionHistory).join(...)` returns six rows unpinned and one row pinned.

Two properties make this better than an interval-aware `primaryjoin`. The generator gets *simpler* — one relationship shape for every parent, no expression varying with `end_open` and `interval`. And the interval semantics stay in `HistoryMixin` beside `valid_at` and `overlaps`, where every other interval decision already lives.

The failure mode improves too. Forgetting the context yields a wrong *shape* rather than a plausible wrong value.

## Decisions

**Join on the key columns alone.** Composite foreign keys join with `and_` over the column pairs. Where the parent has a history table the relationship targets that class; where it has none, it targets the parent's current table, because a table that does not version has exactly one state and the current row is not a guess about the past. Same attribute name either way, so nothing is conditional at the call site.

**The relationship is scalar.** `uselist=False` gives `version.region`, which reads the way someone arriving from `Customer.region` expects. See the limits below for how far the unpinned warning can be trusted.

**Criteria propagation stays on.** `with_loader_criteria` propagates to subsequent loads by default. Turning it off allows a path-based exemption for `Customer.history`, but leaves `joinedload` silently unfiltered:

```
propagate_to_loaders=False   joinedload -> ['North', 'Northern']    unfiltered
propagate_to_loaders=True    joinedload -> ['North']
```

Buying an exemption at the cost of a silently wrong eager load is the wrong trade for a design whose whole purpose is removing silent wrongness. It also makes the rule one sentence: inside a pinned session, every history table shows only the version valid at that instant.

**Statements that name their own time win.** One execution option with two values, set by the helpers on themselves:

- `versions_of` and `timeline` mean *all versions*.
- `as_of` and `changes_between` mean *this instant, not the session's*.

Without it the predicates AND, and a sub-question inside a pinned session silently returns nothing:

```
session pinned to 2025-03-01
   as_of(2025-07-01), no opt-out  -> []
   as_of(2025-07-01), opting out  -> [('Acme Ltd', 7)]
   plain select, still pinned     -> [('Acme Ltd', 3)]
```

This matters because `as_of` names two things: the classmethod that builds a select for one class, and the session context that pins everything. Renaming the context — `binding.at`, `binding.snapshot` — is worth considering on top, but the opt-out is what makes the behaviour correct.

**`as_of()` with no argument means now.** Filtering then only ever happens because someone asked, while "current state across the whole model" stays a one-word opt-in. `valid_at` normalises per class, so one instant works across classes with different `naive_utc` settings.

**Criteria are a plain expression, not a lambda.** Both forms measured identical — one generated statement and three cache hits across four queries at three distinct instants, with correct per-instant results either way. The instant binds as a parameter rather than compiling into the SQL, so the caching concern does not reproduce.

**The option list is built once per context, and covers every history class.** The instant is fixed for the life of the context, so the objects are built at entry and applied per statement. Scoping them to the entities named in a statement is far cheaper but silently misses `joinedload`, which is the same disqualifier as turning off propagation:

```
200 history classes, per query
  plain session                          0.074 ms
  rebuilt each execution                 5.324 ms
  built once, all classes applied        1.762 ms
  scoped to entities in the statement    0.101 ms   <- misses joinedload
```

1.7 ms against a Databricks query measured in tens or hundreds of milliseconds is noise. It is not noise in a lazy-load loop, so the guide should keep steering people at eager loading. A safe version of scoping would have to resolve eager-load paths as well as statement entities, which needs private API and should be measured before adopting.

**A pinned session is read-only.** A session fixed to an instant has no business flushing changes, and the criteria are only applied to selects, so a write would escape the pin entirely.

## Limits to document, not to fix

**A pinned session pins history tables only.** Current tables are not SCD2, so nothing filters them, and a query touching both mixes two moments:

```
session pinned to 2025-03-01
select(Customer) -> [('Acme Corp', 7)]     today's row, not March's
```

**`current()` refuses inside a pinned session.** It is broken there in both configurations, and one of the two failures is silent:

```
session pinned to 2025-03-01
  current(), current_in_history=True   -> []
  current(), current_in_history=False  -> [('Acme Corp', 7)]      today's row
  what the caller probably meant       -> [('Acme Ltd', 3)]
```

With the live row in history, `current()` builds `select(History).where(EndDate IS NULL)` and the pin ANDs `valid_at` onto it, leaving only entities that have not changed since the pinned instant. That is not reliably empty - pinned to an instant before an entity's last change it returns a row - so it silently drops exactly the entities whose history is the reason for the query. With the live row absent from history, `current()` reads the primary table, which the context cannot reach, and returns today's state.

So it raises, with an error naming both readings:

```
current() means now, but this session is pinned to 2025-03-01.
For the version at that instant, select the class directly.
For today, use an unpinned session.
```

Chosen on asymmetry of regret. Refusing cannot produce a wrong answer and is trivial to implement. If it proves too strict it can be relaxed later into "current relative to the session's clock" without breaking any caller, because code that raises starts working. Shipping either permissive reading and getting it wrong means silently answering the wrong question in historical reports.

That "session's clock" reading is the better end state - it is correct in all four combinations, and it fixes `current_in_history=False` too, since a *past* instant does exist in that history table and only *now* is missing from it. It is blocked on a separate question: `current()` is a classmethod with no session in scope, so making it context-aware means either rebuilding the statement inside the listener or moving the call onto the session as `s.current(CustomerHistory)`. Decide that on its own merits, not as a side effect of this.

**`customer.history` narrows to a single version** inside a pinned session, which follows from the one-sentence rule rather than contradicting it. `versions_of` and `timeline` are the way to ask for the whole timeline, and they carry the opt-out.

**The unpinned warning is opportunistic, not a guarantee.** `uselist=False` warns only when the parent actually has more than one version:

```
customer 42 (parent has 2 versions): v.region -> North   warned=True
customer 99 (parent has 1 version):  v.region -> Only    warned=False
```

So a fixture with single-version parents never sees it. A collection-valued relationship is no better — a fan-out is equally invisible on single-version data. The warning is worth having and cannot be the primary defence; the guide should say traversal from a history class is meaningful inside a pinned session and not otherwise. Recommend `-W error::SAWarning` in test suites.

**A self-referencing history relationship works.** A history class pointing at its own class resolves through `include_aliases` on the self-join, and the parent comes back at the same instant as the child:

```
pinned to 2025-03-01:  Acme Ltd   parent -> Globex
pinned to 2026-06-01:  Acme Corp  parent -> Globex Intl
```

The parent company was renamed in September 2025, so this is the point-in-time answer rather than the current one. Keep a test for it, since nothing else exercises an aliased self-join.

## What to build

- `HistoryMixin` keeps `valid_at` and `overlaps`; no interval logic moves into the templates.
- `generate` emits a scalar `viewonly` relationship from a history class to the parent, targeting the parent's history class where one exists and its current class otherwise.
- `Binding.as_of(at=None, overrides=None)` returns a read-only pinned session, with the option list built at entry.
- `versions_of` and `timeline` set the all-versions scope; `as_of` and `changes_between` set the explicit-instant scope.
- Decide what `current()` does inside a pinned session.
- Tests: each load strategy, the override, both opt-out scopes, the unpinned warning, a composite-key join, a self-referencing history class, and a parent with no history table.
- Documentation, detailed below. Every decision here changes what a user has to know, and none of it is guessable from the generated code.

## Documentation

`docs/generated/history.md` loses its hand-written join section and gains the pinned-session form. The rule goes first, in one sentence: *inside a pinned session, every history table shows only the version valid at that instant.* Then a decision table - given what you want, which call do you reach for - because that is the part a reader needs to hold in their head.

Worked examples, each short and each showing its output:

- A pinned session and a traversal: the whole point, in five lines.
- `as_of()` with no argument, and why "now" is an opt-in rather than a default.
- Overriding one entity to a different instant, and opting one out entirely.
- `versions_of` and `timeline` from inside a pinned session, returning every version, next to a plain select returning one.
- `as_of(other_instant)` inside a pinned session, returning its own instant rather than the session's or nothing.
- `current()` unpinned, and the error it raises pinned, with both alternatives spelled out.
- The same traversal unpinned and pinned side by side, with the rename that makes the difference visible. The `North` / `Northern` example is the clearest one and should be the one that appears.
- `customer.history` inside a pinned session narrowing to a single version, and how to ask for the timeline instead.
- A query joining a history table to a current table, showing the two moments in one result, so the limit is concrete rather than a warning in prose.
- A parent with no history table, where the attribute points at the current class and why that is not a compromise.
- A self-referencing history class, where the parent resolves at the same instant as the child.
- Eager loading, with the reason: the pin costs real time per statement, so a lazy-load loop pays it once per load.

The gotchas page gains the two limits that can bite silently: a pinned session pins history tables only, and the unpinned `uselist=False` warning fires only where the data has more than one version, so it cannot be relied on as the signal that a pin was forgotten.

## Done when

A pinned session narrows every history entity across lazy, `selectinload`, `joinedload` and explicit joins; per-entity override and opt-out work; `versions_of` and `timeline` return every version from inside a pinned session and `as_of` returns its own instant; `current()` raises inside one; an unpinned traversal warns where the data allows; and the guide carries the rule, the decision table, and every worked example listed above with its output.
close_reason: Binding.as_of pins a session; history classes carry key-only relationships that the session narrows; versions_of and timeline mean every version and as_of and changes_between mean their own instant; current() raises inside a pin. Guide rewritten with the rule, a decision table and worked examples. The composite-key case is blocked on bd-02s, which is filed.

The decision itself is still open, so this ticket is still about choosing between leaving it, generating a current-row join under an unambiguous name, generating the as-of join where the parent has history, or offering it as a runtime helper.

title: Report the tables whose composite keys make them invisible to relationship inference
description:
`propose_foreign_keys` only indexes a table that has exactly one primary key column. A table whose key spans several columns is therefore invisible as a relationship target, and no reference to it is ever proposed.

That is the right behaviour - matching column pairs by name across a catalog has a far higher false-positive rate than matching single columns, and a reference someone had to think about belongs in the overlay. What is wrong is that nothing says so. The operator sees relationships they expected simply not appear, with no line of output to explain it, and the discovery path is noticing an absence.

`stele infer` already reports what it found. It should also report what it declined to look for:

```
2 table(s) have composite keys; references to them are not proposed:
  dbo.District (RegionId, DistrictId)
  dbo.OrderLine (OrderId, LineNo)
  -> declare those references in the overlay
```

The same list is worth having before any query is run, since it tells an operator whether composite keys are a factor in their catalog at all.

## Scope

Reporting only. Inference does not learn to propose composite references; that is a separate question with a worse error rate and no clear demand.

## Done when

`stele infer` names every table whose key spans several columns, with the columns, and points at the overlay. A test covers a spec containing one.
close_reason: stele infer lists every table whose key spans several columns, with the columns and a pointer to the overlay. composite_key_tables() in infer.py, printed by cmd_infer.

title: overlay.py and profile.py have no tests
description:
Neither module has a direct test. Both are on the main path: the overlay is the one artifact an operator hand-edits, and profiling decides every string width in the replica.

The correlation is worth naming. Every defect this review turned up sits on a path with no test, and the two untested modules are where several of them are.

Specific gaps:

- `write_overlay_stub` output is never round-tripped through `load_overlay` and `apply_overlay`, so nothing checks that what `infer` writes is what the overlay reader accepts. Column names containing YAML-special characters would break the unquoted flow lists the stub emits.
- `apply_overlay`'s merge and replace modes, `add_tables`, and the warning paths are unexercised.
- Profiling has no test of batching, the sampling wrapper, or `profile_warnings`.
- `test_closed_interval_changes_boundary` asserts that a string appears in generated text; it would pass with the boundary logic inverted.
- The read-only engine guard and the `information_schema` parsing are both untested.

## Done when

The overlay round-trips from stub to applied spec in a test, both merge modes and the warning paths are covered, profiling is exercised against SQLite or a fake, and the closed-interval test runs a query instead of reading text.

title: Foreign key target index lets one table claim a key name used in several schemas
description:
`propose_foreign_keys` builds one flat index of key names for the whole spec and populates it with `targets.setdefault(name, (tbl, keys[0]))`. The index is keyed by normalised name only — `_key_names(table_name)` plus the parent's own primary key column name — with no schema component, while table identity everywhere else in the spec is `schema.name`.

So when two schemas both contain a table of the same name, whichever is reached first in `spec.primary_tables` claims every name it generates. A second `Customer` in another schema registers nothing, and every `CustomerId` column in every schema is proposed against the first one. `setdefault` makes this silent: no warning, no lowered score, and the proposal reads exactly like a correct one at 0.80 with "types agree".

Single-schema runs cannot hit this. It appears the first time several schemas are introspected together, which is also the only way cross-schema foreign keys are found at all, so it arrives precisely when the feature starts being used.

## Options

- Key the index by schema and prefer a same-schema parent, falling back to another schema only when the name is unique across the spec.
- Detect the collision and emit both proposals at a reduced score with the ambiguity named in the reason, leaving the choice to the overlay.
- Detect the collision and emit neither, with a warning naming the competing tables.

The second and third keep the resolution in the operator's hands, which matches how the rest of inference treats things it cannot settle from names alone. The first is a guess that will be right often enough to be trusted and wrong without saying so.

## Done when

Two same-named tables in different schemas cannot silently capture each other's child columns, and `tests/test_pipeline.py` covers a spec with the collision in it.
close_reason: The target index maps a name to every table claiming it. A parent in the child's own schema settles the match; with none, every candidate is proposed at half score with the rivals named, and to_foreign_key_specs drops a column two parents claim rather than choosing.

title: Keep dependencies and workflows updated with Dependabot and audited with zizmor
description:
Two supply-chain gaps: nothing proposes dependency or GitHub Actions updates, and nothing checks the workflows for the usual Actions security mistakes.

Add `.github/dependabot.yml` covering the `uv` ecosystem (`pyproject.toml` plus `uv.lock`) and `github-actions`, both weekly with a 7-day cooldown so a release has to survive a week before it is proposed. Group each ecosystem into a single pull request so a week of updates is one review rather than five.

Add `zizmor` to the dev dependency group and a step to `check.sh`, so workflow auditing runs locally and in CI through the same script as every other check. Fix what it reports on the existing workflow: pin both actions to commit hashes with the version in a trailing comment, set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout, and declare explicit `permissions`.

Action versions stay where they are; Dependabot proposes the major bumps on its own schedule.
close_reason: Dependabot config and zizmor step landed; workflow findings fixed

title: Document the pipeline and the generated package in a Material for MkDocs guide
description:
The README is the only documentation, and it carries two jobs badly: it is the first thing a reader sees, and it is also the step-by-step reference for a six-command pipeline. It should keep the first job and hand off the second. Nothing at all covers using the package that comes out, and the least guessable parts are the ones a reader cannot recover from the emitted code.

## Why Material for MkDocs

Markdown sources beside the code, a navigation tree, and code-block rendering with tabs for the Databricks and SQL Server sides of the same example. The alternative is growing the README until it stops being readable in a terminal, which it is currently sized for.

## What the README keeps

An introduction and an overview: what the tool is for, the shape of catalog it assumes, the `model.yaml` / `overlay.yaml` split as the central design idea, the six commands as a diagram, install, and a pointer to the guide. Everything below "Walkthrough" moves.

## What the guide covers

**Overview and setup.** What the tool assumes about a catalog and why. Install, connection settings and their precedence, and a first run end to end against one schema.

**The pipeline, one page per command.** `introspect`, `profile`, `infer`, `generate`, `ddl`, `check`. Each page says what the command reads, what it writes, and which flags change the outcome rather than the presentation.

**What the code actually looks for.** This is the section with no existing equivalent, and the reason someone would trust or distrust the output.

- Introspection: the four `information_schema` queries, the Inspector fallback and when it fires, how `X` is paired with `X_history` and how the history table's key is derived.
- Profiling: what is sampled, why an observed maximum is a lower bound on a declared width, and why lengths are rounded up to buckets.
- Primary key inference: the three rules in order — a key affix on either side of the table name, a bare generic name in a leading position, a stem match — with the scores each produces and the bonuses for non-nullable and leading ordinal.
- Foreign key inference: how candidate names are built, that a parent needs a single-column key to be a target, how a parent in the child's own schema settles a contested name, and what happens when none does.
- Validation: what `--validate` counts, and how containment and null fraction turn a name match into evidence.
- The score table, and what `--min-score` does at each threshold.

**Changing the output.** Where each kind of correction belongs: introspection flags for SCD2 shape, `--include` and `--exclude` for scope, `type_override` for widths, and the overlay for keys, relationships, names, and tables the catalog never reported. The rule that `model.yaml` and `models/` are regenerable and the overlay is not.

**Gotchas.** Every schema must be introspected together for cross-schema relationships to be found. `infer` never reads the overlay. `infer` will not overwrite an existing overlay without `--force`. `profile` and `infer` have no schema filter. Composite keys are not proposed. Self-references are not auto-proposed. Complex types do not round-trip.

**Using the generated package.** Binding, the schema token and `schema_translate_map`, one query against both backends, and why Databricks opens read-only.

**Joins and history, worked.** Examples against a model with enough shape to be worth reading: several schemas, a table whose key names run the other way, two tables sharing a name across schemas, a composite key declared by hand, and a history pair. Cover the `history` relationship, each SCD2 helper including what `current` does when the live row is not duplicated into history, and the hand-written join a history class needs because it carries no relationships of its own — see [[bd-nzy]].

**What the types tell you.** What carries the element type through and what stays open, each for a stated reason.

## Decisions this needs

- Whether the docs build runs in CI. A job that fails on a broken link is worth more than the docs themselves.
- Whether examples are executed. `examples/demo_sqlite.py` already runs a full SCD2 story against SQLite; sourcing snippets from a file the tests execute keeps the guide from drifting, which the README's snippets cannot do.

## Done when

A Material for MkDocs site builds from `docs/`, covers the sections above, and the README is back to introduction and overview with a pointer to it.
close_reason: docs/ builds with Material for MkDocs and covers overview, setup, one page per command, the full heuristic and scoring rules, where each kind of correction belongs, gotchas, and the generated package: bindings and schema translation, relationships, history, and typing. README reduced to overview plus a first run. check.sh builds the docs with --strict.

title: SCD2 query helpers return Select[Any], erasing the element type
description:
`HistoryMixin.as_of`, `current`, `changes_between`, and `versions_of` are all annotated `-> Select[Any]`, as is `as_of_all`. Each one returns `select(cls)` or a filtered form of it, so the element type is known at the point of construction and thrown away by the annotation.

The effect is that the typing on `Binding.scalars` and `Binding.rows` does not reach the queries most callers actually write. `binding.scalars(select(Customer))` resolves to `list[Customer]`, but `binding.scalars(CustomerHistory.as_of(ts))` resolves to `list[Any]`, because `Any` satisfies the `Select[tuple[T]]` parameter with `T` bound to `Any`. No error is raised; the type is simply gone. The generated SCD2 helpers are the main query surface, so this is the path that matters.

The fix is `Select[tuple[Self]]` on the classmethods, `dict[str, Select[tuple[HistoryMixin]]]` or a generic equivalent for `as_of_all`. `versions_of` takes `entity: Any` as well, which is a separate and smaller question.

This carries the same SQLAlchemy version constraint as the `Binding` signatures: the one-tuple spelling is a 2.0 form, and 2.1 makes `Select` variadic. The decision recorded on the `Binding` work applies here unchanged — use the 2.0 spelling, add no upper bound, and let a mypy error be the signal if 2.1 ever gets installed.

## Done when

The point-in-time helpers carry the element type, and a test asserts the inferred type with `typing.assert_type` the way `tests/test_binding_types.py` does.
close_reason: as_of, changes_between, versions_of and timeline return Select[tuple[Self]]. current keeps Select[tuple[Any]] because it selects the primary table when current_in_history is false, so the element class is a property of the model rather than the call. as_of_all keeps Any: a type variable there names the element type only for a single-class list and rejects the mixed list it exists for.

title: Rough edges in generated code and around the CLI
description:
A grab bag from a review pass, none individually urgent.

**Generated code**, against the stated bar of reading like hand-written SQLAlchemy: `ForeignKey` is imported into every module whether used or not, and the template always imports `HistoryMixin`, `SCD2Config` and `TYPE_CHECKING`, so a module without history fails a lint someone points at it. Three blank lines after imports when there is no `TYPE_CHECKING` block, one blank line between the primary and history classes. Composite primaryjoins render a space before the comma.

**Runtime:** two functions named `utcnow` with different signatures, and the exported one - `history.utcnow(cfg)` - is not the one `Binding` uses, so a user calling the documented export with no argument gets a `TypeError`. Calling `pin()` twice on one session stacks listeners and duplicates criteria.

**Dead code:** `types.ceil_pow2`, `ColumnSpec.python_name`, and a `bucket_length` call in `profile.py` whose result is discarded.

**CLI:** `ddl --schema` values without `=` traceback. `check` and `ddl` require the package directory's basename to be a valid module name. `naive_utc` is the only `HistoryConfig` setting with no introspect flag, and nothing says so. An `--include` pattern matching `X` but not `X_history` silently drops versioning.

**Inference and overlay details:** three different `min_score` defaults across `infer()`, `apply_to_spec` and the CLI. `infer()` mutates the caller's spec as an undocumented side effect, which also makes `--apply`'s count wrong. An unknown `foreign_keys_mode` silently behaves as merge. `spec_version` is written and never checked. A lowercase `type_override` emits an import of the literal type name and fails at check.

**Profiling:** an all-empty-string column profiles as length 0 and becomes `NVARCHAR(MAX)` with a note telling you to run the profile you just ran. The Inspector fallback drops views while the information_schema path keeps them, with nothing saying so.

**Docs drift:** `ddl-and-check.md`'s sample DDL shows unnamed constraints where the naming convention emits named ones. `pipeline/generate.md` says the output directory is overwritten, but stale modules from a previous run are left in place.

title: Write a prior-art page relating stele to existing tools and research
description:
stele derives its heuristics and its file layout from first principles, and nobody has checked whether the same problems are already solved elsewhere. Two risks follow: reinventing something worse than what exists, and failing to credit work the design is effectively built on.

The deliverable is a documentation page - `docs/prior-art.md` or similar - saying how stele relates to existing tools and research. Not a defensive comparison table; a short honest account of what is solved elsewhere, what stele borrows, and what it does differently and why.

## The bar for citations

Every claim about another project must be checked against that project's own documentation or source, and the page must say which. "Its README states" and "reading its source shows" are different claims and should read differently. Anything inferred rather than verified is either checked or cut - a prior-art page that misdescribes a neighbouring project is worse than no page.

## The six capabilities to research

Each is a separate question with its own literature.

**Generating SQLAlchemy models from a live database.** SQLAlchemy's own `automap`, `sqlacodegen`, the older `sqlautocode`. Also worth a look for shape rather than language: Django `inspectdb`, Prisma introspection, JOOQ's generator, Hibernate reverse engineering.

**Inferring keys and references when the catalog declares none.** This is the axis most likely to have real prior art, and it has both tools and an academic literature. Unique column combination discovery and inclusion dependency discovery are the formal names; Metanome is the best-known research platform, and HyFD, Sindy and Binder are algorithms worth reading about even if no usable implementation exists. Find out whether the containment measure stele uses has a standard name and a standard threshold.

**Recovering string widths by profiling.** Great Expectations, ydata-profiling, and whatever the data-quality world uses for the same job.

**SCD2 query helpers in an ORM.** `sqlalchemy-continuum`, `sqlalchemy-history`, SQL:2011 system-versioned tables, Postgres temporal extensions. The specific question is whether any of them attaches to history tables that already exist in a source system with their own start and end columns, rather than managing tables it created itself.

**One model set addressing two backends.** SQLAlchemy's `schema_translate_map` is the mechanism stele uses; the question is whether anyone else builds a generator on it.

**The regenerate-plus-overlay pattern.** dbt's `schema.yml`, SQLMesh, Terraform's split between configuration and state, OpenAPI and protobuf generator customisation layers. Whether this shape has a name is itself worth knowing.

## What is already established

Two fetches were made before the session's web search budget ran out. Both are grounded in the projects' own documentation.

**`sqlacodegen` stops where stele starts.** It generates declarative SQLAlchemy 2.x from a live database and relies on existing database constraints: its documentation states it does not infer missing primary or foreign keys. A table with no primary key degrades to a bare `Table` rather than a mapped class. There is no customisation layer surviving regeneration and no profiling. On a federated catalog that declares nothing, it produces almost nothing - which is the input stele exists for. Source: https://github.com/agronholm/sqlacodegen

**`sqlalchemy-continuum` is unresolved and should not be summarised from what was read.** Its documentation index confirms a versioning extension that manages its own version and transaction tables and offers querying entities at a given revision. Whether it can attach to pre-existing SCD2 tables with their own interval columns - the only question that matters here - is not answerable from the index. The Basics and Configuration pages settle it. Source: https://sqlalchemy-continuum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

## Method

Do this single-threaded. Fanning it across five agents exhausted a 200-call web search budget without producing a report, and the budget is per session: check `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION` before starting, and spend searches on discovery rather than on re-reading pages already known.

## Done when

A page exists that states, per capability, what already exists and how close it is, with every citation checked and its basis named. Anything that turns out to be solved elsewhere is said plainly, including if the honest conclusion is that some part of stele should be replaced by an existing tool.

title: Replica DDL emits IDENTITY on integer primary keys
description:
Every single-column integer primary key compiles with `IDENTITY` in the replica DDL, because `mapped_column(BigInteger(), primary_key=True)` leaves `autoincrement="auto"`.

```
[H3WidgetId] BIGINT NOT NULL IDENTITY,
```

The replica mirrors data whose keys are owned upstream, so the column must carry the source's values. ORM loads happen to work, since SQLAlchemy's mssql dialect toggles `IDENTITY_INSERT` for them. A bulk load - `bcp`, `BULK INSERT`, most ETL tools - without `KEEPIDENTITY` silently assigns new keys and breaks every foreign key pointing at the table. Wrong data, no error.

The sample DDL in `docs/pipeline/ddl-and-check.md` shows no `IDENTITY`, so the documented intent already disagrees with the output.

## Direction

Emit `autoincrement=False` on primary key columns. In this tool's domain the keys are always upstream-owned, so there is no case where the database should be assigning them.

## Done when

Generated primary keys carry `autoincrement=False`, the replica DDL contains no `IDENTITY`, and a test asserts it on an integer key.
close_reason: Primary key columns carry autoincrement=False, so the replica DDL declares no IDENTITY. Fixed in the template; the rule is unconditional so the generator needed no branch. Landed in its own pull request; the closure rides here because ticket bookkeeping was kept to one process.

title: Reconcile how the CLI resolves Databricks connection settings from the environment
description:
## What prompted this

Connection settings exported in a zsh session were not picked up by `stele introspect`, and the run only succeeded once `--host`, `--http-path`, and `--token` were passed explicitly.

**The cause of that particular run is not established.** Reading the three documented variables works. Exercising `cli._engine` with `databricks_engine` patched out, `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`, `DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH`, and `DATABRICKS_TOKEN` all resolve; the hostname has `https://` and a trailing slash stripped; and a flag overrides its matching variable without discarding the other two. Two explanations remain and neither is confirmed:

- `DATABRICKS_HOST` was set rather than `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`. The Databricks CLI and the Databricks SDK use the first name. `databricks-sql-connector`, whose naming stele follows, uses the second. stele ignores the first entirely.
- The assignments lacked `export`, leaving them as zsh parameters that no child process inherits.

`env | grep DATABRICKS` in that shell would separate the two. That is worth knowing, but it is not a prerequisite for this ticket: each defect below was reproduced on its own and stands whether or not any of them explains that run.

## Defects

**`DATABRICKS_HOST` is ignored.** Someone arriving from `databricks configure` or the SDK already has it exported, and stele reports the connection settings as missing while a usable hostname sits in the environment.

**The missing-configuration path prints a traceback.** With nothing set, `stele introspect` raises `RuntimeError` out of `DatabricksConfig.from_env` and the user gets a Python stack trace. The other missing-value path in `cli._engine` raises `SystemExit` and prints one line. Same failure, two presentations, and the traceback is the one a first-time user hits.

**`DATABRICKS_CATALOG` and `DATABRICKS_SCHEMA` cannot be reached from the CLI.** `DatabricksConfig.from_env` reads both, but `cli._engine` calls `from_env` only when `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME` is unset, and `from_env` raises unconditionally in exactly that case. Confirmed by probe: with `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` set, the resolved catalog is still the `--catalog` value. Since `--catalog` is `required=True` on `introspect`, `profile`, and `infer`, no invocation reaches either variable. `from_env` has no successful path from the CLI at all; it only ever raises.

**There is no file-based source.** Every setting is read from `os.environ` and nothing else. `.env` and `.envrc` are gitignored, but no code reads either. A setting that lives only in a shell session does not survive a second terminal, a new day, or an assignment made without `export` — the last being one of the two unconfirmed causes of the run above.

## Direction

**Two names, canonical first.** `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME` is read first and `DATABRICKS_HOST` is a fallback. The alias is what someone arriving from `databricks configure` or the SDK already has exported, and it usually carries a full `https://` URL, which the existing normalization already strips.

**A project-local `.env`.** Reading one removes the whole class of settings that never reach the process, and keeps a token out of shell history and out of `~/.zshrc`. Take `python-dotenv` as a core dependency rather than parsing the file here: `export` prefixes, quoting, escapes, and multi-line values have enough edge cases to be worth not owning, and it is pure Python with no dependencies of its own. Load once in `main()` before argparse dispatch, with `override=False`, searching upward from the working directory so an invocation from a subdirectory still finds the file at the project root.

**Precedence is one sentence: flag, then exported environment, then `.env`.** An exported variable beating the file is the right direction; it is the one just typed.

**`~/.databrickscfg` is out of scope.** It is the file someone arriving from `databricks configure` actually has, but reading it correctly means profiles, which means depending on `databricks-sdk`. That is too large a dependency for the convenience.

A file source raises the stakes on the catalog and schema defect rather than lowering them. Someone writing a `.env` will put a catalog in it, and it stays unreachable while `--catalog` is `required=True`. Make the two variables work rather than deleting them from `from_env`.

## Done when

`DATABRICKS_HOST` resolves as a fallback for `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`; a `.env` file is loaded with flag, exported environment, then file precedence; missing configuration exits with a single readable message naming all three sources rather than a traceback; and `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` and `DATABRICKS_SCHEMA` are reachable from the CLI.
